                                        nitric acid and evaporation of the solution. ‘The product which is very pure is dried in a
                                        ervaining kettle.

              AMCP 706-177 Black Powder .                                                                                                                                       ’

id   oY + ge                                                                                                                                               oo                    ,
              Preparation:                                                                                                                                                  «

              Willow or alder charcoal, flour of sulphur and 2-3% of water are placed in «a tumbling barrel                                                                                 ae

     ;        and mixed for a short period (sbout 1/2 hour). ‘The mixture is transferred to a "wheel mill" end                                                      t
     ‘                                                                                                                                                             :.
              crystalline potassium nitrate containing 3-5% moisture is added and the mixture ie in: orpoveted             :
                                                                                                                                                                 i
              for ewrerel hours. During the incorporation period the mixture is kept damp (2-3% moisture) by               "
                                                                                                                                                                  ra
              o2°iug water at intervals. The mill cake is then pressed at 6000 psi between aluminum plates.                :
                                                                                                                                                                    *
              The pressed cakes are broken up betveen rubber or wood rolls. ‘The material is screened and toe

              various particle sizes are seperated as desired. ‘he screened material is then trenaferred to

              canvas trays and dried in hot sir ovens at 60°C. If it is desired to glaze the black powder,

              the material before drying is polishe’ by rotation in a tumbling barrel to give it a sacoth

              surface. It is next screened to remove the dust. The smooth particles are then placed in «

              woogéen barrel and rotated with graphite. The miterial is egain screened to remove the excess

              graphite, and dried. Naterial finer than #0 U. S. Sieve is not grephited.

     i                                                         WARNING                                                         :
     :
                    The batches of black power mst be of sufficient size to cover the bed of the "whee) mill.”                   -
              If the wheels run off on the bare bed, explosions usually result.                                                      ‘
                                                                                                                                       .
              Origins                                                                                                                 ‘

Bes  |                     The exact date of the discovery of black powder is unknown. Historians ettribute ite dis-   a
 a
                     covery to che Chinese, Hindus or Arabs. ‘The Greeks used it during the 7th Century. Marcus       \ .

                     Graecus in the 9th Century and Roger Bacon in the 13th Century described compositions siniler             .
              ‘to the present powder. Beginning with the 16th Century, the composition of black powler con-

                    taining potassium nitrate, charcoal and sulfur has rersined unchanged with respect to the pro-
                   portionality (75/15/10) of the ingredients.

              Destruction by Chemical Decomposition:

              Black powder can be desensitized by leaching with water to dissolve the potassium nitrate.

              The washings must be disposed of separatcly because the residue of sulfur end charcoal is com-

              bustible but not explosive.                                                      ;

              References: ’

              (a) Ph. Neoum, Nitroglycerine and Nitroglycerine Explosives, @altimore, 1928.

              (b) F. W. Brown, D, H, Kusier and F. C. Gibson, Sensitivitv of Explosives to Initiation by

              Electrostatic Discharges, U. S. Department of the Interior, Bureau o:  es        9  .

              (c) Also see the following Picatinny Arsenal Technical Reports on Black Powder:

              ‘See footnote 1, page 10.

                tion { Labor’              :

                      To @ cooled mixture of 73.5 gm of 100% nitric acid, 446.2 gms of 106.2% sulfuric acid and
                60.0 gu of 96.1% suifuric acid, 3 gus of the original (or rediatilied) 1,2,4-butanetriol was
                added dropwise with agitation for a period of thirty minutes. the temperature of the reaction
                mixture ves kept at 0°-5°C. When the agitation was completed. stirring waa continued for one
                end one-half hours. ‘The aixture was poured into ice water, ani the resulting ofl suspension
                was extrected with three 100 milliiiter portions of «ther. The com ethb er eixn trace ts vd ere
                washed vith water, then with « 5% acdium bicarbonate solution and finally with water. The nau-
                tralised extract was dried with anhydrous calcium chloride and then the ether was evaporated.
                The yellow oil was dried in a vacum desiccator over anhydrous celetum chloride antil the mate-
                rial wes brought to constant weight.

                Origin:

                      1,2,h-butanetriol wes Yiret synthesized by Wagner and Ginsberg in 1894 by oxidising allyl

                carbinol with potassium peroanganate under mild conditions (Ber 27, 2437). Recently the U. S.
                Tubber Laboratory, under the direction of P. Tawney, devised a new synthesis carried out with
                allyl acetate and formaldehyde to give 1,2,h-butane triacatate which ves ceadily hydrolysed t:
                butanetriol (U. S. Rubber Company Guarterly Report, May 1948). Working with pure 1,2,4-butane-
                ‘\wiol prepared by an improved technique of the Wagner method, the U. S. Ruval Laboratory in

                1948 nitrated the butanetricl on a laburetory and a pilot plant scale (Refersuce a).

                        Compatibility with Metals:

                           Dry ~ Aluminum, stainless steel, mild steel, mild steel coated 'rith acid-proof black paint

                        and mild steel plated with nickel or zinc are unsffected. Copper, magnesium, magnesium-aluminun
                        alloy, brass and mild steel plated with cadmiur. or copre: are siightly affected.

                        steel coated wit. acid-proof black paint and mild rteel plated with copper, cadmium, nickel or
                        zinc are slightiy affected.

                        Origin:

                              Developed by the British during World War II as RDX and beeswax. Subsequent changes in the
                        United States replaced beeswax with synthetic waryet, chansed the granulation of RDX and improved
                        the method of manufacture.

                        Destruction by Chemical Decomposition:

es a 2 2 ee vow ee “ee      RDX Coexposition A-3 (RDX/wax, 91/9) is decomposed by adding it slowly to 25 times its weight
                        of bofling 5% sodium hydroxide. Boiling of the solution is continued for one-half hour.

                                                           Composition B                        AMCP 706-177

aa                 Compatibility with Metals:

                         Dry - Magnesium, aluminum, magnesium-aluminur allvy, mild steel, ctainless steel, mild steel
                   coated with acid-proof black paint and mild steel plated with zinc or nickel are unaffected.

                   Copper, Lrass and mild steel plated with copper om cadmium are slightly affected.

                         Wet - Aluminum and stainless steel are unaffected. Crpper, brass, mild steel, mild steel
                   coated with acid-proof black paint and mild steel plated with cedmiu:, copper, nickel or zine
                   are slightiy affected. Magnesinm and magnesium-sluminum alloy are more heavily affected.

                   Preparation:

wae r ec eee ne a         Water wet RDX is added slowly with stirring to molten TP” melted in a steam-jacketed kettle
                   at a temperature of 100°C. Some water is poured off and heating and stirring are continued un-
                   til all moisture is evaporated. Wax is then added and when thoroughly mixed, the composition
                   is cooled to a satisfactory pouring temperature. It is cast directly into ammunitior components
                   or in the form of chips when Composition B is to be stored.

                   Destruction by Chemical Decomposition:

wvivwe                    RDX Composition B is decomposed in 12 parts by weight of technical grade acetone heated to

P e                45°C, While this is stirred vigorously, there is added 12 parte of a solution, heated to 70°C,
                   of 1 part sodium sulfide (NepS‘9Ho0) in & parts water. The sulfide solution is added slowly so

                   that the temperature of the acetone solution does not rise above 60°C. Alter add‘tion _ com~
                   plete, stirring is continued for one-half hour.

      POOR                                                          tion:

      OOP) Capone’                                             Tn manufacturing Composition C-3, the mixed plasticizing agent is heated in a melting kettle
                                                         at 100°C. Water-wet RDX is added and heating and stirring sre continued until all che water is
      ee ee og eT ee wee Ere ene dina inane              evaporated. This mixture is then cooled and hand pressed into demolftion blocks or special iten
                                                         emrani tion.

                                                              Composition C-4 in presared by hand kneading and rolling, or in a Schrader Bowl mixer, RDX
                                                         of 4k micron size or less with the polyisobutylene-plasticizer previously made up in ether. ‘the
                                                         thoroughly blended explosive is dried in air at 60°C and loosely packed by hand temping to ite

                                                         maximum density.

                                                                ne

                                                              Developed by the British during World War II au a plastic explosive which could be hand
                                                         shaped. It wea standardized in the United States during World Wer II and subsequent development
                                                         led to mixtures designated (-2, C-3 and C-4.

                                                         Destruction Chemical De           ition:       .

                                                              Composition C-3 is decomposed by adding it slowly tc u solution composed of 1 1/4 parts
                                                         sodium hydroxide, 11 parte ‘mter, and 4 paris 95% alcohol, heated to 50°C. After addition of
                                                         Composition C-3 is complete, the solution is heated tc 80% and maintained at this temperature

                                                         for 15 minutes.

                      /mmonium nitrete and acetic anhydride are placed in a flask and, vhile the mixture is stirred            .               fats          >
                                                                                                                                      H
                  at T5°C, the following three liquide are introduced concurrently and proportionately: ecetic an-                   :      :         we     :
                  hydride, concentrated nitric acid, and «@ solution of hexamine in glacial acetic acid. The fine)                ‘
                  mixture is held for a short time at 75°C, diluted with water to 30% acetic acid, and simmered to        :                 a                      ;
                  hydrolyze unstable reaction by-products, woich are a mixture of various nitrated and acetylated                    ;
                                                                                                                                                                   i
                  derivatives of hexamine fragments. After simmering, the slurry is cooled and the precipitated            vik
                                                                                                                                                      ve
                  cyelonite removed by filtration. The yield is 78% of the theoretical amount (2 moles) of cyclo-    a“ 5
                  nite melting at 199°C. By dissolving the ammonium nitrate in the nitric acid, a continuous pro-
                                                                                                                     Nee”
                  ceas, based on 3 liquids, is possible.                                                                            i

                       The product is recrystallized from acetone, or cyclohexanone, to (a) remove acidity, (b)}                '

                  control particle size and (e)} to produce stable A-2K. ‘The preparative procedure described                 .

                  stove, the Bachmann or Combination process, yields cyclonite containing 3-84 HMX.

                               bs                                                                                                                          trae

                     First prepared by Henning in 1899 (German Patent 104,280) and later by von Hertz (U. 8.                                                    i

                  Patent 1, 402,693) in 1922 vho recognized its value as an explosive. Not used on a large scale                                            .
                  in explosive ammunition until World War II.

   An smmoniacal solution of an amine is prepared by adding aqueous formaldehyde to amsonium
   hydroxide. ‘The rate of addition of formaldehyde is regulated to maintain a solution tempers-
   ture of 30° to 35°C.                         .

          Sodium nitrite is dissolved in water and the solution or slurry is then poured into tae
   previously prepared emine-exmonia solution end totally dissolved by stirring. This solution
   is chilled to below 0°c.

          Into a mixed acid solution, previously prepared by dissolving concentrated nitric acid
   in water and adding concentrated sulfuric acid, all chilled to -9°C, there is added the cold
   axing-nitrite solution below the surface of the acid mixture. The sddition is regulated to

   take 20 to RD minutes.

          The resulting foamy head of cyclotrimethylene trinitroramine is allowed to ¢2t over the
   icy spent liquor for 1/2 hour and is then collected on a sintered gless funnel end weshed to
   neutrality. ‘The scist cyclotrimethylene trinitrosamine is removed from the funnel and air-

   dried on filter paper. ‘The dry crude product melts at 106° to 107°C. Recrystallization from
   iscamyl alcohol gives e pure compound meiting at 105° to 107°C.

            in;

           Cyclotrinethylene trinitrosamine was discovered in 1888 simulteneously by Griess and
   Harrow (Ber 21 (1868), p. 2737) and by Mayer (Ber 22 (1888), p. 2883) when sodium nitrite
   was allowed to react with hexamethylene tetramine Tn acid solution. This compound was later
   studied by Duten and Scherff (Aon 268 (1895), p. 218) and by Delépine vho determined ite heat
   of formation, vhich wes negative (Bull Soc chim (3) 15 (1536), p- 1199). Because cyclotri-
   methylene trinitrosamine could be made at first in very poor yield only, it was a long time
   pefore it received consideration for practical application as an explosive. However. the
   study of cyclotrimthylene trinitroeamine wes continued and investigations were msde es tc
   its bebavior in mixtures with other substances (Prof. D. G. Rémer "Report on Explosives,”
   BIOSGP 2-HEC 5742).

   Destruction by Chemical Decomposition:

           Cyclotrimethylene trinitrosamine is easily decomposed by icid cr alkaii and even by

   boiling in water.

     1,3-Diamino-2,4,6-Trinitrobenzene (DATNB)  AMCP 706-177

me

w e  Preparation:

a        Fifty grams {50 gm) of ary styphnic acid was added to 200 gm of anhydrous pyridine with

S e  stirring. The resultine slurry was stirred for an additional 30 minutes. The yellow product,
     dipyridinium styphnatce, was collected by filtration and washed with approximattly 100 milli-
     liters of diethyl ether. The product was dried over phosphorus (V} oxide, at room tempera-
     ture, for,5 hours. Yield of 77 gm (Qu¢), melting point 168° to 170°C (literature me) ting
     point 173 C)-

         To 50 milliliters of phosphorus oxytrichloride, 29.8 gm of the dipyridinium styphnate were
     added in emi portions, with stirring. The reaction mixture was then warmed on a steam bath
     for 15 minutes. This solution was quenched in 500 gm of ice water. The light yellow precipi-
     tate was separated by filtration and washed with water until the washing was neutral to lit-

     Tus. ssi of 1, 3-dichhoro-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene 20.4 gm (98%), MP 130° to 131°C (literature

     MP 126°C).
         A suspension of 3 gm of 1,3-dichloro-2,4,6-trinitrovenzene in 9 milliliters of sbsoli.te

     methanol was prepared. ‘This slurry was cooled to o°c, and dry ammonia was bubbled iio the
     stirred suspension. After 20 minites the reaction mixture was allowed to warm to room tem-
     perature, filtered by suction and washeé wi*h methanol and ether until a negative Beilstein

     test for chloride ion was obtained on the wishings. Yield of 1, 3-diamino-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene
     2.5 em (9T#),» MP 288° to 290°C (literature MP 285°C).

     Origin:

         DAINB, also called 2,4,6-trinitro-1l, 3-diamino-benzol or 2,4,6-trinitro-phenylenediamine-
     (1,3), was first obtained by Noelting and Collin in 1884 (Ber 17, 260) and also by Barr in
     1888 (Ber 21, 1546) from 2,4,6-trinitroresorcin dimethylether Th contact with ammoniacel
     aicohol for several days. J. J. Blanksma obtained the same pro:uct in 192 by reacting
     either 2-chloro-2,4,6-trinitroanisole or 3-chloro-2,4,6-trinitrophenetol with ammoniacel
     aicohol (Rec trav chim 21, 324) and from 2,4,6-trinitroresorcin methylethyl etuer with ammo-
     niacal eleohol (Rec trav chim 27, 56 (1908)).

        Meisenheimer and Patzig in 190€ prepared DAINB in the form of yellow needles, MP 280°C

     from 1,3,5-trinitrobenzene . ydroxylamine and sodium methylate in methyl alcohol (Ber 39, 25h0).

     The product wes slightly soluble in glacial acetic acid but poorly soluble in other solvents.

     It decomposed into NH3 end 2,4,6-trinitroresorcin when boiled with dilute NeOH or KOH (Beil 13,

     60).

          Korner and Contardi prepered DATNB by the reaction of either 2,4-dichloro-1,3, $-trinitro-
     benzene or 2,4-dibromo-1,72,5-trinitrobenzene with ammoniacal alcohol at room temperature or
     better by heating to 100°C (Atti R. Accad Lincei (5), 171, 473 (1903)); (5) 18 I, 101 (1909)).
     A method of preparation by prolonged reaction of Nenitro-N-methy1-2, 3,4,6-tetrani troaniline

     with a saturated ammonia solution was reported in 1913 by van Romburgh and Scheers (Akad
     Amsterdam Vers] 22, 297).

           C. F. Van Duin obtained DATNB melting at 301°C by reacting a concentrated aqueous ammonia
     solution with Nenitro-N,N,N-trimethy1-2,4,6-trinitrophenylenediamine-(1,3) or with Nenitro-

     N-wethy1-N-pheny1-2,4,6-trinitrophenylenediamine-(1,3) (Rec trav chim 38, 69-100 (1919)).

     later Van Duin and Van Lenrep reacted concentrated aqueous ammonia with 2,4,6-trinitro-3-
     aminoenisole or 2,4,6-trinitro-3-aminophenetol to obtein UATNB melting at 237° to 288°r (Rec
     truv chim 39, 147-77 (1920))- In 1927 Lorang prepared the same compound by boiling 2,4,6-

     tri itro-l, 3-bis (| -nitcoethyl ureido) benzene with water or by heating it with smmoniacal
     aicohol ina tube st 100°C (Rec trav chim 44, 649) (Beil #17, 2 II 33)-

Origin:

    First prepared and etudied by We. H. Rinkenbach in 1927 (Ind Eng Chem 19, 925 (1927) and
later by Rinkenbech and H. A. Aaronson (Ind Eng Chem 23, 160 (1931)) both of Picatinny Arsenal.

\Jeed in propeliant compositions by the Germans during World Wer II.

Lestruction by Chemical Decomposition:

    DBGN is decomposed by adding it slowly to 10 times its weight of 16% sodium sulfide
(3wpS* 9820). Heat is liberated by this reaction but this is not hazar ious if stirring is

maintained during the addition of DEGN and continued until solution is complete.

ee                            Dinitropropanol was nixed with chloroform (1320 williliters) and the mixture heated to
                      ‘
                         boiling. ‘The distillate was collected in & water separator. At first the distillate was
e e                      cloudy and this was dried with calcium chloride before being returned to the system. When
                         no more water was collected in the water separator, the mixture was cooled to rcom tempera-
e e                      ture and the separator removed. Fumaryl chloride was introduced, followed by the aluminum
                         chloride which wes added in four equal portions. Air was blown into the flask for a minute
                         to effect mixing, and the reaction sustained itself without the adcition of heat for one hour.

                         Steam was gradually introduced so that the reflux temperature was reached 2-1/2 hours after

                         the beginning of the reaction. After 3 hours of reflux, the hot liquid was poured jnto a
                         bucket. As cooling took place the slurry was vigo .sly agitated until it finally set up at
                         room temperature. This material was broken up and mixed with dilute ice cold HCl. The solid
                         product was collected on & sintered funnel, washed with water and ith heacuc. The crude
                         material was recrystallized from methanol to give a product melting at 66°C (urcorrected),

                         but after storage for several days the melt‘ng point was 89°C.

A methylene chloride solution of dinitropropanol (0.02 mol ‘n 15 milliliters) was mixed                  :

with 0.01 mol of succinyl chloride. To this solution 0.003 mcl of crushed anhydrous aluminum ~           .

chloride was added. It was necessary to cool the reaction vessel due to the vigorousness of              .

the reaction. After 25 minutes at room temperature the reactior. solution wor refluxed 1-1/2             0

hours. Fine needle-like crystals formed upon cooling and adding hexane. The crystels were                ‘

slurried in dilute hydrochloric acid and on recrystallization from methanol gave a 93% yield             :

of INPS (melting point 85° to 85.6°C).                                                                   3

       AMCP 706-177         Glycerol Monolactate Trinttrate (GLIM) Liquid

            tion:

 .     Glycerol monolactate (GML) _s prepared by heating a glycerol lectic acid mixture containing
  ve
       hd excess lactic acid at 116°C for 112 hours with dry air bubbling through the liquid. ‘he
  oat
       product which contains 0.67% free acid is carefully mixed with 6 parts of 40/60 TI /B2 90,
Pos.
       maintained at 20°C, stirred for 1 hour, cooled to 5°C, and poured on ice. It is  ¢
aa
       with ether, weter-washed, adjusted to pH 7 by sheking with a sodium bicarbonate solution, and
 oe
       egein water-washed tnice times. It ie then dried with calcium chloride, filtered end freed

       of ether by bubblivg vi‘h eir until minim] loss in weight is obteined. The product has a

       nitrate-nitrogen conte.t of 13.43% (theoretical 14.1% N). Another batch, prepared from “ML

       obtained from glycerol-lactic acid containing 6.5% excess glycerol, had a nitrete-nitr’ge.

       content of 14.30%, corresponding to a mixture containing 5.5% nitroglycerin. It 1 not con-

       sidered practicable to prepare the pure GLIK.

       int

       The preparation of a nitrated ester of lactic acid and glycerol, by nitrating a glyceryl             .

       lactate vith nitric and sulfuric acids, for use in explosives, was reported in 1931 by Charles       a

       Stine and Charles Burke (U. S. Patent 1,792,515).                                                    _¢  .

,      The preparation of glycerol monolactate by heating glycerol with equimolar proportions of

       a lactic acid ester of an alcohol boiling below 100°C (ethyl lactate) was patented by Richie

       H. Locke in 193% (British Patent 456,525 end U. S. Patent 2,087,960).

The rew materials used in this process are cheep and available; the first three reactions

proceed smoothly, rapidly and in good yield (70% overall), and only the third requires high

pressures. The reaction of ethylenediamine with carbon dioxide at about 220°C and 820 atmos-

pheres has been worked out and is more satisfactory for the preparation of ethyleneurea than

the use of chlorethyl carbonate or urea and better than the reaction of acetic anhydride and

ethylenediamine to yield N,N’-diacetyl-ethylenediamine which can be treated in a way similar              .

to the above to yleld Haleite.

Ethyleneurea is very easily nitrated, with strong nitric acid (95%). st ordinary teoperature,             -  ae

and in a very short time, and the dinitroethyleneurea produced appears .. u,drolyze, yielding             ‘

Haleite, immediately after solution in water at 95°C. Doth the nitration and hydreiycis are                  ee oc

practically quantitative.

was 1935 before its value as an explosive was recognized. Standardized Curing World War II                   .

as a military explosive.

Destzuction Chemical Decomposition:

Haleite is decomposed by addition to hot, dilute sulfuric acid. Nitrous oxide, acetalde-                            j

hyde and -thy.ene glycol are evolved. Haleite is also decomposed by addition to 5 times its    eo                   a

weight of 20% sodium hydroxide.                                                                ‘                    :

                                    HBX-1; HBX-3

ee

C n     Preperation:

Ber          HBX explosive mixtures are prepared by melting INT in a steam-Jacketed melt kettle equipped
        with a mechanical stirrer. Water-wet ‘dX is added slowly with stirring and heating until all
w w     the water ie evaporated. Aluminum is added, and the composition is stirred until uaiforn.
        D-2 wax and calcium chloride are then added. ‘The desensitizer wax, also known as Composition
D H
        D-2, consists of dh@ paraffin and other waxes, 14% nitrocellulose and 24 lecithin. ‘The mixture
        is cooled from approximately 95° to 100°C to a temperature considered suitable for casting
        (the lowest rracticable pour temperature). BX can also be made by adding the calculated
        Cmount of TNT to Composition B to outain the desired proportion of RDX/TNT. The appropriate

        weights of the other ingredients are added to complete the mixture.

        Origin:

w w

o w         Developed during World War II, as relatively insensitive mixtures, by adding 5% desensiti-

        zer to Toroex II, for high blast explosive applicetions.

        References3 34

              (a) 0. E. Sheffield, Blast Properties of  Losives Containing Aluminum or Otner ietal

        Additives, PATR No. 2353, November 1956.

aan.         (b) S. D. Stein, G. J. Horvat end 0. B. Sheffield, Some Properties and Cnaracteristics
        of HBX-1, HBX-3 and H-6, PATR No. 2431, June 1957.

ewe         (c) L. C. Snitn and S R. Walton, A Consideration of RDX/Wax Mixtures as a Substitute for

        Tetryl in Boostere, NOL Memo. 10,303, 15 June 1949.

        Report No. 1502, 26 July 1950.

     en the 24ST-3 aluminum panels occurred with the projectile nose always pointed toward C° and

       i            Preparation:

       ae               The HEX compositions were prepared by blending the appropsiate weight of the dry ingredients

       wow          in a Patterson-Kelly twin-shell blender for et least 30 minutes.

       eee               0 alternate procedure for 100 to 200 gram batches used a "Cradle-Roll" mixing device.
                    This device consisted of a half-barrel type container constructed cf woud and lined with an
       ey           electrical conductive material. A plastic roll was allowed to move over the ingrediente by
                    remote control action of the container. The roll action prevented caking of the mix but had
                    no adverse effect on the particle size of the ingredients. The period of time required to
                    obtained a uniform and intimate mixture was approximtely fifteen minutes.

       e e    .     Origin:

                    The development of "slow-burning"” explosive mixtures which would produce increased blast

                    effects in enclosed or nearly enclosed spaces directed attention to thelr use for possible

                    military application. In 1950 Picatinny Arsenal developed a high capacity filler for 20mm

                    projectiles consisting of 85/10/5 RDX/aluminum/desensitizer which was more powerful than stan-

,      :            dard tetryl filler. However, in comparison with MOX type explosives, there was little doubt

       ’            as to th. superior performance of the MOX mixture. HEX (hig. cvergy explosive) mixtures were

       :            developed at Picatinny Arsenal in 1953 (Ref a) as superior high bic-t Compositions suitable

       :            for use in small caliber projectiles.

Preparation:

       To prepare hexanitro-oxanilide, ficst prepare tetranitro-oxanilide as described herein

under the entry "2,4,2',4'~Tetranitro-oxanilide (TNO).”

      A 1.5 liter round bottom flask is equipped with a stirrer of the type which causes a dowm-
ward swirl. The flask is jacketed for hot and cold water. 187 grams of nitric acid of speci-

fic gravity 1.49 (commercial grade) is placed into the flask and 100 grams of sulphuric acid
is added to the nitric acid under agitation... T:« mixed acid is coole2 to 10°C. 29.2 grems of

tetranitro-oxanilide is slowly added to the mixed acid under rapid agitation maintaining the

temperature at 80-100C. After the addition of the INC is completed (approximately 25 minutes)
the temperature is raised to 85°C over a period of 2 hours and heJd at &5°-90°c for one hour.
The hexanitro-oxanilide (HNO) "slurry" is filtered on a Euchrer ‘unne) and purified as cx-
plained under "Tetranitro-oxnilide.”

Origin:

     A. G. Perkin in 1892 obtained hexanitro-oxanilide directly by heating to boiling a solution
of tetranitro-oxanilide in e mixture of sulfuric and nitric acids. He also prepared the same
compound from oxanilide by the action of a boiling mixture of fuming nitric and sulfuric acids
(J Chem Soc 61, 462 (18925).

(a) Ome hundred gress of pure resorcin is fused in « porcelain casserole and immediately

poonu # gr lase s pld ate. After cooling, the cake is ground in c mortar to pass a U. S. Stan-

Gard No. 6 mesh sexseen. Four hundred grems of 96 percent nitric acid in a one pint capacity

Dewar jar is stirred mechani    while carbon dioxide snow is added in small pieces. When                  .

the temperature falls to -20°C, grams of the granulated resorcin is added in saall quenti-

ties, Simltaneous addition of soJ]id carbon dioxide as required prevents a rise of tempera-

ture of more than 5 degrees throughout the entire experiment. Five minutes after the last

portion of resorcin is introduced, the mixture is further cooled to minus 50°C, and finally

drowned vith vigorous atirring in Tie times its volume of cracked ice, in water. This mix-

ture is allowed to stand for one hour and the product then filtered, washed, and pertially

dried, weight 43.6 grams. ‘The crude 4,6-T8R is purified by first dissolving the product in
an aquecus 5 percent sodium hydroxide solution {17.4 grams of sodium hydroxide in 340 ce of

warm water, into vhich is gradually stirred 0.10 mole (4.0 grams) of sodium hydroxide dis-         Secor        ‘

solved in 67 ce of vater, 3tirring is continued for five mimtes. After settling, the vhite

     (c) A 0.0278 mole (3.56 grams) quantity of the 4,6-DaR prepared under (a) above, is dis-

persed in 270 cc of wa‘er by vigorously beating with a motor stirrer. After heating this
dispersion to 90°C, the 0.05 mole of lead hydroxide prepared above in elurry form is intro-
duced in small portions. Agitation is continued for three hours at 90°C. ‘The basic lead

Origin:

Both the 2,4- and 4,6-dinitroresorcin were ad scribed in some detail by Weseleky, Benedikt

and Huol in 1862 (MII, 323). Typke prepared the 4,6-din‘troresorcin in 1883 by hydrolyzing

the nitretion product of resorcin diacetate (Ber 16, 551). A wore direct and economical

method of preperation suitable for production scale manufectuce was developed during World

War II by the British (Ministry of Supply Pouch Item W-154-2ie, "Mrnufacture of 4,6-Dinitro-

resorcin and Lead 4,6-Dinitroresorcinate"). This procedure consisted of preparing 4,6-

dinitroresorcinol by direct nitration of granulated resorcin and allowing the product in slurry              ;

to react with an excess of leed hydroxide at 90°C. This basic salt can be prepared in two                    ~

forma: (1) a microecrystalline, yellow, low-deneity form and (2) a denser, brick-red form.

Bot products have the same chemical composition and the eame sensitivity to impact (PATR

14L8, September 19b4).

    Preparation: (Laboratory Method) (k)

        @. Cool to helow 0°C, 5¢ gm of 964-100% nitric acid placed in a 300 milliliter Erlenmeyer

    Pyrex flask provided with a thermometer and immersed in an ice-selt mixture.

        bd. Introduce in small portions, 10 gm of d-mannitol, while svirling the flask to break up

    any lumps of mannite which might form. Keep tne temperature below 0°c.
or

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           Cy
         ce After solution is complete, add 100 gm of concentrated sulfuric acid from a dropping
    funnel, swirling the flask in an ice-salt mixture to keep the temperature below 0°C.

       ad Filter the resulting porridge-like slurry through a filter paper previously hardened

    by treatment with mixed aci¢.

        e. Rinse the precipitate directly on the filter with water followed by dilute aqueous

    sodium carbonate and finally with water. (The resulting crude mannitol hexanitrate gives

    16.2% N an cctermined by the nitrometer).                             .

          f. Dissolve the crude mannitol hexanitrate in boiling alcohol and filter through a water-
    Leaved funnel.

          g- Bring the filtrace to boiling and gradually add hot water until the appearance of the
    first turbidity.

        4. Cool in an ice-salt bath, 3  te and dry the crystels. (Yield should be about 23

    gm of material, melting it 112°-113°C and having 18.58% N, the nitrogen being determined by

    t.2 nitrometer. Theoretical yicld would be 24.2 gn.)

    Origin:

        Mannitol hexanitrate was discovered in 1847 hy Ascanio Sobrero who recommended it as a sub-

    stitute for mercury fulminate in percussion caps (Coup rend. 1yAL7. 121). It is the hexanitric

    ester ofmi tel which is widely distributed ‘. nature, particularly in it= vlant Frwrinus

    ornus. N. Sokoloff, a Rusaian chemist, investigated che explosivé properties of my end recon-

                         Chemistry:

                               Mercuric fulminate readily decomposes in the presence of aqueous solutions, chlorides, car-
                         bdonate and many other materials. Ike to the presence of sumll amounts of mercury, formed by
                         exposure to light or elevated temperatures, it readily forms amalgams with copper, brass and
                         bronze, thus components containing these metals must be protectivel, coated if used with ful-
                         minate.

                Five gm mercury is dissolved in 25 cc 6f nitric acid (sp gr 1-42) without agitation, and     O
            this solution poured into 50 ce of 90% ethyl alcohol, resulting in a vigorous reaction,                                                                                                                                                          Ben

            atte by en volutd ion e of wd hite fumes and subsequent appeerance of fulminate crystals.
            fomes then appear as precipitation of the product accelerates, and then white fumes again are
            evolved as the reaction moderates. After about 20 minutes the reection is over; water is
            edfed, and the crystals are repeatedly washed, by decantation, with weter to remove all acidi-
            ty. ‘he product is purified, rendered white, by solution in strong emmonium hydroxide, foi-
            lowed by reprecipitation with 30% acetic acid.

                ne

                Mercury fulminate wes first prepared by John K. von Lowenstern (1630-1703) and in 1800 its

            preparation and properties were first described in detail by Edwerd Howard in « peper presented

            to the Royal Society of London (Phil Trans, 204 (1800). It was 1867 before the compound wes

            used es an initiating agent, when         jovel invented the blasting cep and used mercury ful-

            minate to detonate nitroglycerin (British Patent 1345 (1867)).

            Destruction by Chemical Decomposition:

                 Mercury fulminate ig decomposed by adding it, while stirring, to at least 10 times its
            weight of 20% sodium “hiceulfate. Some poiscnous cyanogen gas may be evolved.

    Pee.
                       Metriol (trimethylolmethylnethene) te obtained by the following prcecedure, based on work
                   by Hosneus (Annalen 276, 76 (1893):

:      :                    Into a 5 liter round bottow Ziask in weighed 2700 gms of water. To this are edded 267 gms
                       of 36% formaldehyde and 60 gms of propionaldehyde. The mixwure is stirred for a few seconds.
it                     To the mixture iz added 150 gms of calcium oxide previously sleked with 600 gma of vater.
                        The mixture is heeted in bolling water Yor four hours, and then allowed to cool spontaneously
                                                                                                                                  .
                        overnight. After filtering off the insolutle calcium hydroxide, the solution is heated and                ,
                        treated with a saturated aqueous solution of oxalic acid to precipitate all the calcium. The
                                                                                                                                 :
                        precipitated calcium osslate is filtered off, and the pale-yellow filtrate concentreted as
                   ‘ guch as possible on the steam beth to a thick lemon-yellow syrup. After diasolving in sbso-                  ;

                         lute alcohol, the solution is filtered and concentreted in the ateam beth to about twice the        oy

                        voltum of the concentrated syrup. The solution ie then chilled in a cold box to hasten cry-             ‘

                       stallizction. After allowing it to warm up to just above 0°C, the mixture is filtered. ‘he                .
                                                                                                                                 .
                        resulting product is not sufficiently pure and is recrystallized from absolute alcohol. The

                       melting point of the product (40.3 gm) is then about 196°C (Hosseus gives 199°C).

                       Metricl is nitrated by cerefully mixing it with 3.5 parte of 65/35 HNO2/H,90, mintained
                   at 20°C, stirring for © minutes, cooling to 5°C, and pouring the reactiof mixture on ice. It

                   tes extracted with ether, water-washed, and adjusted to pH 7 by shaking with 2 sodium bicar-

                   ponate solution and again water-washed three tines. It ia then dried with calcium chloride,

                   filtered, and freed o: ether by bubbling with dry air until minimal rate of loss in weight is

                   atteined. “=: yield is  of the theoretical. The product has a nitrate-nitrogen contert

                   of 16.35% (calerlated: 16.47%). Ite refractive index at 25°C is 1.4752.

                   ins

    ‘                    MIN, according to Italijn sources, was first prepared and patented by Bombrini-Parodi-           .
                                                                                                                       i
                   Delfino Company of Italy unasr the name "metriolo." A German Patent cr 1927 also describes          Ne
                   the preparation and gives some properties. This compound was known in Trance before World
                   Wax II under the name of "Nitrorentaglycerin" and Burlot and Thomas determined its heat of
                   combustion (Ref b).

   . Preparation:

         The various ingredients used in the preparation of MOX explosives are coated separately as
   follows:

         Dichromated Atomized Aluminum - Seventy-five grams of chemically pure grade sodium dichro-

   mace is dissolved m in 1i50l0liliters of water at 100°C under mechanical agitetion. Six hun-

   Gred grams of the atomized aluminum powler is added gradually (2 to 3 minutes) end stirring

   ie continued for helf an hour. The dichromated metal is filtered, washed with water (15 to 20

   times) until the washings show only a slight cloudiness with silver nitrete. ‘The water-vwet
   product is then dried in an oven at 50°C. The dried material is hand-rolled to reduce eny

   conglomevates, and blended tefore use.

        Wax-Coated RDX - Eighteen grams of molten Be Square Special Wax (manufacturer 5 180° to

   185° Fahrenheit grade amber) is added to 582 grams of finely divided RDX (water precipitated

   from acetone solution) in a water slurry under mechanical agitation. The temperature of the
   wex-RDX slurry is mainteined above the melting point of the wax (about .O°C). ‘The stirring
   ie continued for half an hour. Aiter cooling to 50°C, the wax-comted RDX is recovered ty
   filtration in a Buchner funnel and dried in air. The RDX thus coated and presumed to be 3%
   waxed ROX or a 97/3 RDX/wax mixiure is hand-rolled to crush any conglomerates formed, and

   blenied by hand before use.

         INT-Coated Barium Nitrate - Thirty grams of TNT in alcohol solution is added to 270 crams

   of barium nitrate in an @iccnol slugry under agitation. The temperature of the TNT-berium
   nitrate mixture is maintsined ut 80°C and stirring ia continued until most of the alcohol is

   evaporated. The coated material is spread in 4 thin layer on a tray to dry in air overnight.

   The barium nitvate thus coated with 1O% THT ig reduced to an intimte mixture by haud-rolling
   ard blending before use.

i  INT-Costed Potassium Nitrate - The TNT-costed potassium nitrate is prepared by the sem
   procedure aa 28 used Tor coating barium nitrate.

i  ADK/INT-Coated Ammonium Perchlorate - The ammonium perchicrs‘e ig conted by dissolving the
   Sppropriste weights
                        ani  n hot + ‘cohol. After add... the ammonium perchlorate,

   th. ‘cry ig stirred until most of the solven: is evaporated. The treated amroniun perchlo-

   rate spread on a tray to dry overnight. Agglomerates forme during the process are crushed

   by hand-rolling and blending ths mixture before use.

          INT-Voatcd ROX - Sixty grams of rolten INT are added to a water slurry of 540 grems of

   finely divided Rix (water precipitated from acetone solution) under mechanical agitation.

   The temperature of tac INT-RDX slurry is mainvaine1 at about 90°C and etirring is continued
   Yor helys an hour. Alter cooling to about 30°, the TNT-coated RIX is recovered by filtration.

   The ROX thus treated, and presumed to be 10% coated or a 90/10 RDX/TNT mixture, is further
   blended vy hand after rollirg to crush any eggregutes formed during the process.

         ‘ae MOX explosive mixtures are prepared by blending the appropriete weights of the dary
   Ingredients in a Patterson-Kelly twin-shell blender for at lest 30 ninutes.

         tion of Nitrocellulose fron Cotton Linvers:
         oratory Procedure}

          Nitration: Second cut cotton linters, previously dried to a moisture content of iecs than

    0.5%, are nitrated by immersion in mixed acid under the following conditions:

        Ratio of Mixed Acid to cotton 55 tol

        Composition of Mixed Acia (approximate)

         a. for 12.6% N: Hp80), 63.5%, HNO; 216, HpO 15.5%

         b. for 13.4% Ns HoS0, 68%, HNO: 22%, Ho0 10.0%

wa      Temperature of acid at the start         3bP

        Time of nitration                        2k minutes

           During the nitration period the mixture is turned over occasionally to keep the acid homo-
    geneous. The mixture is then filtered on a Buchner funnel with suction for about three rin-
    utes and then drowned rapidly with strong hand stirring in et least 50 volumes of cold ‘mter.
    After the nitrocellulose has settled, most of the water is decanted and fresh water edded.
    The nitrocell lose-water mixture is boiled and the acidity adjusted to 0.25% to 0.50% as fipSd,, -
    The sour boil is continued for at least 24 hours for pyrocellulose and at least 46 hours for
    gun-cotton. Additional boiling with changes of water are made in accordance with the govern-
    ing specification (JAN-N-2h4).

        Pulping: The nitrocellulose is then pulped in a leboratory Holiand-type psper beater.

    En   sodium carbonate is added to keen the reaction faintly alkaline to phenolphthalein.

    Pulping is continued to the desired degree of fineness.

          Poaching: After washing the nitrocellulose from the beater, the mixture is filtered and

    the product boiled for » hours with fresh water while stirring mechanically. From time to

    time a little cc‘. carbonate solution is added to maintain the mixture faintly .ikaline | >

    phenolphthalein. The water is decanted and the boiling continued. According to the specifi.

    cation, the total boiling treatment with poachi. is as follows:

    230

                             1 hour boiling without sodium carbonate
    ie ie de                 1 hour boiling without sodium carbonate.
                  Each boil is followed by settling and change of water.

    Rew                Washing: The nitrocellulose is then washed by mechanical agitation with water. A minimum

    ew eR Fe      of two washes are given. Ifa sample taken after ths water washes gives a minimm test of
                  35 minutes in the 65.5°C Heat Tesc and 30 minutes in the 134.5°C Heat Test, the nitrocellulose
                  ia satisfactorily stabilized. Otherwise additional washes si.ould be given.

    v e           Origin:

    we me eee          Cellulose occurs in nature. It is wood fiber, cell well and the structural materisi of all
                  plants. Cotton fiber is pure cellulose. Nitrocellulose was discovered about 1847 by C. F.
    | v           Schonbein at Basel. id R. Bottger at Frankfort-on-the-Main independently of each other when
                  cotton was nitrated. 1. J. Pelouze had nitrated paper earlier (1538) and was probably the

                  first to prepare nitrocellulose.

                         oxylin or collodion, which is soluble in a mixture of ether and ethanol, contains from

    e w           84 to    nitrogen. It is used in the manufacture of ceiluloid and in composite blasting

    roe           explosiv.c.

    e y                      celluiose, a type of nitrocellulose of 12.64 nitrogen content, comp: *y suluble ia =
                  mixture of 2 parts ether and one part ethanol, was developed tv Mendeleev ( .i-1895). ‘this
    w e           material, when colloided, formed the first smokele.s powder for military use in the United
                  States (1898).
    wor
                       Guneotton for military purposes 1 ..y contains a minimum of 13.35% nitrogen. Js is only
                  slightly Soluble in ether-ethanol, but completely soluble in acetone. Principal use ia in
                  flashless powders and as flame carriers. 14.14% N nitaocellulose represents a theoret) cal

                  limit.

    aa ae <            In the manufacture -f propellants, there is used a mixture of pyrocellulose and guncotton
                  (b’ Jed nitrocéliutose) of 15.15% to 13.25% nitrogen content.

    a             Testrurtion by Chemical Decomposition:

                       Nitrocellulose is decomposed by adding it, with stirring, tc 5 times its weight of 10%
                  sodium hydroxide heated te 70°C. Stirring is continued for 15 minutes after all the nitro-

                  céllulose pas tee. added.

ee          Glycerine is usually nitrated at 25°C, or below, by adding it very slowly to a well agitated
       mixture of nitric and sulfuric acids, e.g-, 40/59.5/0.5, nitric acid/sulfuric acid/water, us-
       ing an acid/glycerine ratio of approximately 6. Agitation of the reaction mixture is accom-
       plished by use of compressed air. A vapid temperature rise, or appeararce of red fumes, auto-
       matically requires dumping of the charge, immediately, into a drowning vessel filled with
       water. After all the glycerine has been added to the nitrator, agitation and cooling are con-
       tinued until the temperature drops to about 15°C, and the charge is then run into ea separator

       where the NG rises to the top, and is run off to the neutralizer. The nitroglycerin is
       washed first vith water, then with sodium carbonate, and finally with veter. ‘The resultant
       NG when washed with water, produces washings which do not color phenolphthalein, and itself
       is neutral to litms paper.

                 ins

                Nitroglycerin vas first preparcd in 1846 or 1847 by Ascanio Sobrero, an Italian chemiat
            (Mem Acad Torino (2) 10, 195 (1847)). For several years after this discovery, nitroglycerin
            attracted litte interest as an explosive until Alfred Novel in 1364 patented improvements in
            its manufacture and method of initiation (British Patent 1813). Nobel gave the name dynamite

            to mixtures of nitroglycerin and ron-explos ive absorbents, such as charcoal, siliceous earth

            or Kieselguhr (Critish Patent 1 (1867)). Later developments led to gelatine dynamites.

            ammonia dynamites, and so cclled straight dynamites. The first propellants using nitrogly-

            cerin vere called ballistite (Nobel, British Patent 1471 (1688)) and Cordite (/bel ard Dewar,

            British Patents 5624 and 11,664 (1889)).

            Destruction dy Chemical Dec      <tion:

                 Mitroglycerir is decomposed by adding it slowly to 10 times its weight of 18% sodium sul-                       .
            fide (NaS- 9859). Yeat is liberated by this reection; but this is not hazardous if stirring                         :

            ie maintained during the addition of nitroglycerin and contiried until solution is complete.                      :

          itn                  Four hun¢ ed gus of dry guanidine nitrate is added in small portions to 500 cc concentrated

                          sulfuric acid at 10°C, or below. As soon as all cryatals have disappeared the milky solution

                          is poured into 3 liters of ice-water, and allowed to stand until crystallization is complete.

          pry     .       The product is filtered, rinsed with water, and recrystallized from about 4 liters of boiling

                          water, yield about 90%.                                         .

   -                      origin:                      .

          Y                     Nitroguenidine was firet prepered in 1677 by Jousselin, but it was 1900 before it found
                          use in propellant compositions. During World War I, nitroguanidine was used by the Germans
                          as an ingredient. of bursting charge explosives.

          PERE

                          Destruction by Chemical Decomposition:

          SFE

          N E                   Nitroguanidine is      decomposed by dissolving in 15  times ite weight of 45%  sulfuric acid  at
                          root temperature and         warming the solution until gas  is evolved. Heeting is   continued for  one~
                          half hour.

             Preperation:

             A total of 675 gm 37% formalin is added to 150 gm nitromethane conteining 2 em potassium

R G          carhovate heat-hvtrate. The “rst 2CO ga formalin is added vlowly, keeping the          ture

E E          below 30°C, and then the heat of reaction is allowed to raise the tesperetotu60r°eC, and
             the mixture then heated two hours at 90°C. ‘The reaction mixture is then concentrated at re-

             @uced - es" «re and diluted, and this process repeated several times to remove formaldehyde.

             After the .inal concentration the cooled mixture is filtered and the crystalline product recry-

Ww OR ON     stallised from alcoho) and then severy1 times from ether and dried.

                   The nitrated poduct is then obtained by nitrating 50 gm nitroisobutylglycerol with 300 gm

             mixed acid (60/38/2, sulfuric acid/nitric acid/water) below 15°C for 1.5 hours.

             Origin:

e e          This explosive (also called Trimethylolnitromethane Trinitrate, Nitroisobutanetriol Triri-

             trate, Mitroisobutylglycerin Trinitrate and incorrectly but widely used Nitrolsobutylglycerol

          ‘  Trinitrate) was first described in 1912 by Hofwimmer (2 ges Schiess - Sprengstoffw 7, 43

ORO          (1912). Hofwimmer frepared the compound by the condensation of 3 moles of formal       with

             1 mole of nitromethane in the presence of pctassium bicarbonate, the subsequent nitration of

R H          the product. ‘The explosive can now be prodfu romce cokd e, air, and natural gas.

AMCP 706-177            Nitrostarch [smolition Explosive (NSX)

The nitration of starch proceeds with the formation of hexanitro starch according to the                 :

following equation:                     iz                                                               ‘

2CgH005 + SHNO—% C oF, (OWD2)¢ + 6820

Tapioca starch is considered the best for nitration purposes, although other starches give

fairly stable products. The starch, pretreated to remove oils, fats a-d water scluble in-

purities, is dried and screened. Feeding of the dried sterch into stainlces steel nitrators

containing mixed acid (62%-63% HNO. and 37%-3%             ) is done elowly vith constant agitation      .
of the mixture. The heat evolved gust be con ed by cooling coils. The nitrated starch

is separated from the spent acid, vwaahed with « large amount of water and centricuged. Finel            ‘  Te

@rying is on trays heated to 35°-hO°C with air. ‘This product is so sens eveintaiv stae tic              .

Gischarge might cause explosion.

      Hitrostarch demolition explosives contain a high percentage of nitroatarch, an oxidizing

agent, mineral ofl, a stabilizer and/or other ingredients.

Origin:

Kitrostarch was first prepared in 1833 by Branconnot, who called it xyloidine (Am chin

phys [2] 52, 290 (1833)). 1. J. Pelouse studicd xyloidine further end reported ite explosive

properties (Compt rend  713 (1838). It found military use in the United States during

World Wars I and II as    ting explosives end as an ingredient of burating charges and priz-

ing compositions.

Performance of PB-RIK as Booster:         (b, a)

      Ten 2.75 inch HEAT Ml Rocket Heads were unaffected in performance by storage at 71°C for
28 days. Thus, PB-RDX wes not desensitized by contact with TNT-bearing explosives. Tetryl,
similarly used, becomes desensitized when stored in bursting charges at elevated temperatures.

      In addition, 108 modified M307Al 57 mm projectiles were fired for performance againat
armor. Fach round contained a PB-RDX booster pellet. There was no evidence in these firings
that the projectiles were inadequately boostered.

a                                         Preparation:

                                             The purchase description sheet for polystyrene-bonded RDX (X-PA-PD-1088, 25 October 1956)

                                          requires that the PB-RDX shall be a mixture of RDX, coated and surrounded by a homogeneous
                                          mixture of polystyrene and dioctylpnthalste. The specified percentage of RDX shall consist
                                          of a mixture of 73% Type 3, Class A RDX and 25% Type B, Class E RIX. The grenuletion of the

                                          unpressed composition shall be as follows:

a

a ee                                      Through U. 5. Standard                                ‘

                                                    Steve No.     Minimum 4 =| Maximum %

                                          6                       100     as
                                                                  60      -
                                          12
                                                                  --      2
                                          20
                                                                          )
e e                                       35                      --

a                                             Two methods have been reported for the preperation of PB-RDX (Reference: Los Alamos Scien-
                                          tific laboratory, Contract W-7405-Ing 3% with U.S. Atomic Energy Commission, Report No. LA-
a                                         1448). ‘The earlier wethod employed a Baker-Perkine type mixer to blend the componensa. This
                                          procedure gave a product with good pressing charecteristics. However, the molding composition
                                          was nonuniform in granulation and tended to be dusty. ‘The slurry method of PB-RDX preperation            we
                                          gave a product which was uniform, free-flowing and dustless. In addition, PB-RDX granulated

                                          by the elurry method exhibited vatisfactory drying, handing and pressing charactéristics.

                                              Te final procedure incorporating the better features found from the study of such veriabdles
                                          as solvents, solvent/plastic ratios, lacquer addition and temerature, agitation, ROX particle
                                          size distribution, dispersants and rosin additive, was as fol.ows (Reference ce):

                                              Forty-two and five-tenti.s grams (42.5 em) of polystyrene and 8 ce dioctylphthelate were
                                          aiseolved in 200 ce toluene in a lacquer dissolver. Steam was introduced into the jacket
                                          until the temperature reached 65°C. The lacquer was agitated constantly until it was ready
                                          to be added to the granulator. This lacquer contained a i:h ratio of plastic-plasticizer to

                                           toluene.

                                             Four hundrea and fifty grams (450 gm) of RDX and 4500 grams of BA0 (ratio 1:10) were added
                                          to the grenulator. The agitator was set for L00 rpm and the temperature was raised to 75°C

                                          by introducing steam into the jacket. The temperature differential between the lacquer solu-
                                          tion and the RDX/water slurry was 5° to 10°c.

» ii                                          The lacquer solution was poured through the clerging funnel into the grenulator. As soon
                    ‘                     as the lacquer was added, a solution of gelatin in water was added, end che mixture wae agi-

                                          tated until the lacquer was well dispersed in the RDX slurry (approximately 5 minutes}. Granu-

                                          lation took place at this point. Steam wus introduced again into the jacket to distill the
                                          solvent until the temperature reached 98°C. Conling water was then run into the jacket to
                                          eool the batch to 40°C. ‘The coated material from the granulator was collected on a Buchner
                                          funnel and dried in a tray at 70°C for 2k hours. Temperatures below 70°c did net furnish

                                          enough heat, but a temperature of 80°C produceé stickiness and caking of PB-RDX.

rs                                        Origin:

                                              An explosive consisting of RDX coated with polystyrene plasticized with dicetyphthalate

                                          was initially developed in 1952 for the Atomic Energy Conasission by Los Alamos Setentific
                                          laboratory of the Universit; of California (Contract W-7k05-Eng 36 with U. S. Atomic Energy

Commission, Report No. LA-1448). ‘The specific formletion of 90/8.5/1.5 RIM/polystyrene/

dioctylphthclate was subsequently standardised by Loe Alamos. This explosive, originally

designated PRX, has been redesignated PB-RIX. The detailed requirements for the present
polystyrene-bonded RDX(PB-RDX) are given in purchase description X-PA-PD-1088, 25 October 1956.

we se ee                      The earlier’ procedure used for the manufacture of PETRIN was that developed at Alleghany
                       Bellietics Laboretory. In this process, called the "A process,” 80% HNO. and the solid pen-
               .       taerythritol were charged to the reactor and 80% Hp>80, wen added slowly ét a rete to permit

e w                    control of temperature at 0° to 5°C. This mixture wes bela for a 2-1/2-Lour reaction period,

                       then drowned in water and filtered to give a cake containing both the tri- and tetra-nitretes

                       of pentaerythritol. The cake was dissolved in acetone and neutralized in saclution with an-

                       tmontu.. carbonate, after which the PETA ...s precipitated by the addition of weter. After fil-
                       tration, the PETRIN was recovered from the filtrate by stripping off the solvent under vacuum.
                       Yields by this process averaged about 404.

               t             An improved process, calied the "B process," used the same primry reaction procedure but
                       e different work-up procedure. After the reaction holding perici, water wes addgd to dilute
tee                    the mixed acid and the batch was extracted in situ with methylere chloride. The organic

OR Ee                  Layer was separated, neutralized with aqueous sodium bicarbonate, and stripped of methylene

                       ehloride under vacuum to yield the product directly. Yields by this process were sbout 50%
                       and quality of the product was mich improved over that of the "A process."

                             The "C process,” currently in use, involves essentisily the simultaneous synthesis and
                       extraction of PETRIN from the reaction mixture. Methylene chloride approximately equal to

RE A                   the to.al weight of the other components is added to the reaction mixture before the sulfuri:
                       acid. After a .siteble time following the addition of sulfuric acid, the solvent is removed
                       and re;..aced by fresh solvent one or more times. The combined extrects are neutralized and

                       conce.tretec. Because of their initially relatively large volume, PEIN .... be re-oved by

                       filtration. from the concentrated PETREY solution before the final solvent is stripped.  Yields
                       by this process have been 60% to 65%.

                       Origin:

                             The nitretion preducts of pentaerythritol or itc derivati.+s containing not more than three
                       KOg Groups were patented for use as explosives, propellants or ignition materials in 1936

                       (German Patente 636,432 and 638,433; CA 31, 1212 (1937)).

B E                          A process in which pentaerythritol monoacetate was converted to penteerythritol trinitrate

                    a  monoacetate, which was then saponified under carefully controlled conditions to PETRIN, was
                       reported in 1954 (N.S. Marans, Db. B. Elrick ard R. F. Preckei, J Am Chem Soe Tu, 130k).
ree
                       -STRIN was also prepared by the nitration of penteerythritcl with a mixture of Bot HAO, and

     Preparation:                      (a)

     HOCH2C(CH2NO3) 5 + CHy = CHOUCL + Coligh(CH3)p ——

          pentaerythritol           aerylyl     dimethyl

     trinitrate (PETRIN)           chloride      aniline

             MW 271                 MW 90.5       MW 121

     (O,NOCH,) ,CCH,OCCH =CH, + CgHigN( CH) HCL _——_

     pentaerythritol trinitrate mono-        dimethylanine

     acrylate (PETRIN acrylate)              hydrochloride

                 MW 325

     The original synthesis for PETRIN acrylate employed trifluoroacetic anhydride and glacial

     acrylic acid as the acrylation agent for PETRIN. Thege two maveriels were charged to a re-

     action vessel and the initial reacticn was controlled by the slow addition of PETRIN at a

a    temperature of 10° to 15°C. Following a period of one hour, the batch was drowmed in water,

     precipitating the PLIRIN acrylate. This solid was separated by filtration, dissolved in chlo-

a    roform, and neutralized in solution with sodium bicarbonate. The product was then crystel-

a    lized during e period of 16 hours at o°C and dried under vacuum to remove traces of solvent.
     The vield for this process was about 60%.

a         A significant improvement in yield (to about 74%) and purity (approximately 984) was
     realized by the substitution of methanol for chloroform and crystallization of the product
     from the solution without neutralization, residual acid being removed by washing the filter
     cake with water.

           Because of the high cost and hygroscopic nature of trifluoroacetic anhydride, a new pro-
     cess, based on dimethylaniline und scrylyl chloride, was considered. This process is cur-
     rently under development in ine Rohm and Haas Chemical Processing facilities and is not con-
     eidered optimm. Yields averaged 46% and product purities averaged 93.5%.

     PETRIN Acrylate Propellants:

oo   PETRIN acrylate could be used ag & monopropellant because it has a specific impulse of

     214 lb-sec/1b and a burning rete of 0.2 in/sec. ‘he addition of an oxidizer increases both

a    the impulse and burning rate.           .

     A composition which preesntly appears most promising is as followa:

     PEYRIN acrylate (> 97% purity), ¢          Composition To
     Triethylene glycol “sinitrate, %
     Glycol diecrylate, %                       3.5 (binder)
     Ammonium perchlorate, %
e e  Hydroquincne, %                            11.8 (plesticizer)

                                                2.9 (crosalinker)

                                                §1.0        oxidizer)

                                                0.014 (polymerization  inhibitor)

     Measured specific impulse 236 lb-sec/lb, at density of 1.3.

                                        Pentolite            * 10,                   AMCP 706-177

        Preparetion:

OOK           Pentolite is manufactured by either the slurry method or coprecipitation of PEIN and TNT.
        In the slurry nethod PEIN, in water, ie stirred and heated above 80°C. ‘INT is added and when
i e     wolten, it coats the particles of PEIN. The slurry is cooled with rapid etirring and the sepa-
        rated granules are collected on a filter and dried below 75°.

a aaa)        In \oprecipitation, PETN and INT are dissolved separately in acetone. The aclutions are
        mixed an@d the explosives are precipitated aimultaneousl; by pouring the mixed solution inte
        cold water under vigorous agitation. The urecipitated solid is collected on a filter and
        dried in air.

a       in:

              Standardized during World War II, with the 50-50 PEIN/INT mixture being the more important
        for bursting charges and booster-surround charges.

    AMCP 706-177  Picramide (TNA) (2,4,6-Trinitroan:line)

    Preparation:

         Five grams of picryl chleride were dissolved in 180 milliliters of avsolute methanol.
    The solution was then satur®.ed with anhydrous, gaseous ammonia. The time required vas
    approximately 30 minutes. The amino derivative precipitated in 75% yield (3.5 gm) melting

    at 190°C (literature MP 189°C).

    Origin:

         Picramide (2,4 o-trinitroaniline) was first prepared in 1554 vy Pisani who treated picryl
    chloride with aw onium carbonate (CR a 853). The use of picramide, as a brisant explosive,
    was patended by Chemische Febrik Griesheim 26 May 1894 (German Patent 84,628). Meisenheimer

    and Patzig reected trinitrobenzene with hydroxylamine in cold alcohol solution to obtain

    picramide (Ber 29, 2534 (1906)). Witt and Witte obtained the compound by nitrating @ eolu-
    tion of aniline in glacial acetic acid or concentrated SO), at about 5°C with concentrated
    HNO., (Ber 41, 3091 (1908}}. Holleman gives details of the prep ation from p-nitroaniline
    and” from acetanilide (Rec trav chim 49, 112 (1930)).

    Reference: 58

          (a) William H. Rinkenbach, "The Heats of Combustior. and Formation of Aromatic Nitro
    Compounds," J Am Chem Soc 52, 116 (1930).

     all rate -f reaction, below 10.4 molar the rate falls off rapidly. while above 10.4 molar the

     rates «: both the oxynitration reaction anu various side reactions, such as direct nitration,
     increase rupidly. The range mentioned above seems, ‘n general, to give the lowest proportion
     of neutral nitro-compounds to nitro-phenols : ith, ut the same ting, an adequate rate of ox, ni-

     tration. The oxynitration solution must be fortified frequently, or, preferably, contiriously

     with ~Itric acid. Strengths of nitric acid between 95% and 3% are beat. due io the smaller

     increase in reaction volume than if weaker acid were used. ‘The uce of absolute nitric scid

     requires that its direct contact with liguid benzenc be avoided.

     the proportion of neutral nitro-compounds +c nit‘ phenols and amount’ of colored Ly-produc.s.

     cesses vher> an excess of benzene ig use se rate of agitetion is important.

     over 4 daial:’ wide range. Concentrations of 0.3, to 0-5 mole of mercuric nitrate per liter
     of oxynitratic.. solution have been found to cive satisfactory results in most cases.

     venzene at rc-om temperature, the saturated sol..tion is separated from excess benzene and csir-
     culated thro gh a heaicd coll; it is then cooled to room temperature «..a agitat. 1 again. with

     evaluuting this process, the rate of formation of dinitrophenol per liter of reacting solution
     in the col] ‘* determ':ed; 7O gm of dinitropheno’ per liter per hour Is represer tative perfor-
     mance. ‘The diniv-s:.enel is, of course. nitrated to plerite acid.

       Origine

       The possibility of employing ternary uixtures to obtain explosives having greater pover

       and higher brisance then binary mixtures vis               by the enalysis of Russian 76 mm, aruor-

       piercing high explosive rounds (PATR No. 1311, 17 July 1543). The Russian type ternary explo-

       sives, based on the composition and laboratory studies cf such mixtures, were indicated to be

       effective        fillers. In conducting « preliminary study of castable ternary explosive

       mixtures suggested by the Russian fillers, @ mixture consisting RoDf X/PERIN/TNT, designated

       PTX-2 was developed which bad explosive and physical properties offering considerable advan-

       tage for wilitary applications (ATR No. 1360, 2/ October 1943; and 1379, 11 January 1954).

            A PPX-h composition, prepared by the addition of Heleite to 30/70 Pentolite, also offered
       promise but because of border-Line stability in accelerated stability tests, PEX-h must be
       proven by long term storage to be acceptebdle for use in standard emmmnition.

Preparation:
                                                                                                   cs
     Explosive PVA-', a semi-plastic composition of Canadien origin, consists of 906 RDX, &%
polyvinyl acetate and 2% dibutylphthelete (DP). ‘This formation vas developed by Ir. Bathur-
lend of Shevinigen Chemicals, Ltd. In evaluating various types of Polyvinyl acetate comear~
elelly available in the United States, a type obtained from Union Carbide and Carbon, under
the industrial named or designation “AYA” wes the mor+ promising coating for RIX in the pro-
portions RIax/PYA(AYAT)/rEP 92/6/2.

     A practical method of preparing this composition was by the addition of a solution of the
coating agent to an equeous ROX slurry. Based on the quality of the product and the pellet
Gansities obtained, a procedure of adding an acetone solution of PVA + DEP to a hot water
slurry of RIK, under agitation, wis adopted as standard.

                Preparetion:

                1 alcohol is mixed vith acetic anhydride. ‘The mixture is cooled to -5°C and the
                nitric acid is added slowly while the waes is being stirr<’. The teupereture is c-atrolled
                by the rate of acid addition so that when <!1 the acid bas been edded the temperature coes
                not ris: above 20°C.  .                           :

                  When the nitration is complete, the wixture is drowned by allowing a fine stream . the

                ayrupy Mgquic to flow from the nitrator and mix intimately with a large stream of weter. This

                causes the product to precipitate in a fine state.

                me finely divided precipitate ic purified by boiling in frequent changes of water.

                Origin:

                    ‘Te firat preparetion of polyvinyl nitrate was reported in 1929 by solution of polyvinyl
                alcohol in concentrated sulfuric acid and treatment with nitrating acid at e temperature not
                over 50°C. (German Patent 537,303). Later patehts issued relative to polyvinyl nitrate in-

                cluded U. S. Patent 2,118,487 (1938) and Gersen Patent 737,199 (1943).
