       Prepere the following aqueous solutions:

           a. 5¢ NaN,, sodium azide, 50 ce

           bd. 254% AgMOy, silver nitrate, 25 cc

The silver nitrete solution is placed in # 200 cc conductive rubber beaker equipped with «
bard wood stirrer operated by an air motor. The sodium azide solution is placed in a sepere-
tery funnel fectened in a ring stand above the beaker containing the silver nitrate. A long

cord (10 ft) te rhstened to the stopcock of the separatory funnel so thet the funnel can be

exptied by remote control. ‘The sliver nitrate solution is now stirred very repidly end the
sodium azide is slowly run into the nitrate solution. Stirring is continued for 5 minutes.
The contents of the beaker are filtered through folded filter peper end washed free of sodium
azide end silver nitrete vith distilled water.

                                                                                                  i

      Silver azide should be stored under water in a conductive rubber container.  This prepare-  eee
tion will yield approximately 7 grams.

      The preparation should be conducted under a hood and behind « berricade. the product ob-.   o r
tained by the above procedure hes a very fine particle size, almost colloidal. Very fine sil-
ver azide is safer to handle and is just as efficient end stable as the large, coarse orystel-    a e
line material (Ref bd). When a thin film of fne silver azide is precipiteted on mercury ful-
minate. tetryl, etc., these substances are as efficient weight for veight es pure silver aside

(Ref g). White silver azide is less affected by light then mercury or lead azide (Ref h).

Long colorless crystals which explode on breaking are obtained from ammooium hydroxide...

                                                                                                  re

Origin:

                                                                                                  “4

Silver azide was first prepared in 1690-1 by 7. Curtius (Ber 23, 332; Ber 2h, 3344-5) by
passing hytrezoic acid (HN.) into neutral silver nitrate solution. Taylor andRinkenbech pre-
pared pure "collodial"      tes and showed its sensitivity depends upon ite particle size

(Army Ordnance Pa 82h (1925). Silver azide ves found in a detonator of foreign ammunition for
the first time fn 1945 (Ref 4).

Ordnance, Vol 5, p. 82h (1925).

   AMCP 706-177                             Tetracene                                                ~             |

   (Rinkenbach and Burton, Army Ordnance 12, 120 (1931)).

         Tetrecene is prepared by dissolving 5 gms of eminoguanidine dinitrate in 30 cc of water,                     ©.

   cooling to O°C and mixing with a sclution of 2.5 gms of sodium nitrate in 15 cc of water. ‘the
   temperature iz maintained at about 10°C and 6.5 em of acetic acid is added. The tetracene

   separates out and is washed with water, alcohol and ether. It is then dried.

                                                                                                             haem

          Tetracene may also be prepared by placing aminoguanidine sulphate and sodium nitrite in a                                             ‘
   large beaker and adding water her ed to 30°C. ‘The heat of reaction causes the mixture to boil;
   after standing for two or three hours the separated tetracene is filtered off, washed thoroughly                   :
   and dried.

:  Origin:

                                                                                                             ae

   Tetracene was first prepared in 1910 by Hoffman and Roth (Ber 43, 682) who also studied its            °

!  chemical reactions and determined ite structure (Hoffman et al, Eer 43, 1087, 1866 (1910); Ber            ;

:  bh, 2496 (1911); and Ann 380, 131 (1911)). W. H. Rinkenbach and 0.  ton made an extensive                 ‘

‘  ®tudy of tetracene and described its manufacture and explosive properties (Army Ordnance 12,           .

   120 (1932)).                                                                                              :

   Destruction by Chemical Decomposition:                                                                    i

   Tetracene is decomposed by adding it to boiling water and continuing boiling for some time                ‘

   to insure complete decomposition.                                                                         .

            Purification: The TNC is placed in hot water (95° to 100°C) and boiled for five to ten

        Origin:

             The preparation of Tetranitrocarbazole (TNC) was first reported in 1880 by C. Graebe (Ann
        202, 26 (1880)) who nitrated carbazole with 94% nitric acid. Similer procedures were followed
        byR. Escalee (Ber ZI, 2596 (190h)) and P. Zierch (Ber 42, 3800 1909)) However, G. L. Ciami-

        cian and P. P. Silber observed the formation of four isomeric TNC's when acetyl carbazole was
        treated with fuming nitric ecid (Gazz chim ital i2, 272 1682), In 1912 and 1913 patents were

        issued to the dyestuff manufecturer, Caselle and Company, cov: ring the preparation of polyni-

        trocarbazoles (German Patent 268,173 and French Patent 464,53). The Casella process of

AMCP 706-177                     Tetrenitrocarbazole (INC)                                      —
                                                                                                          7
preparing polynitrocarbazoles by dissclving carbazole in sulfuric acid and treating the solu-

tion of sulfonic acids with strong nitrating agents is essentially the process used today in

the United States. he crude product, thus prepared, contains principally 1,3,6,8-tNe (Ww.
Borsche and B. G. B. Scholten Ber 50, 596 (1917) and about 10% of the 1,2,6,8-INC isomer
(D. B. Murphy et al J Am Chem Soc 75, 4289 (1953). ‘TNC was used in explosives by the Germans

during World War II.

i        Oxani lide:

ee Sc          Two parte of oxalic acid are mixed with one part of aniline in a round bottom flask. ‘The
         mixture is stirred and heated until the reaction is complete as evidenced by the cessation of
oi.      effgrve cence. ‘The mass is cooled to room temperature, poured into several volumes of water
         (21°-24"%c), filtered on a Buchner funnel and washed free of oxalic acid with wter and then
i        washed free of aniline with acetone. ‘The oxanilide is air dried to remove the acetone and

C e      then dried at 100°-110°C.

         fetranitro-oxanilide (10):

               A 5 liter round bottom flask is equipped with a stirrer of a type which wil? produce a
         aownverd "swirl." The flask is surrounded with a water Jacket for hot and cold water. Fif-

         teen hundred grams {1.5 kilograms) of 96% plant grade nitric acid is placed into the flask.
         Five hundred (500) grams of cmnilide is slowly added to the acid under rapid agitrtion while
         the temperature is maintained below 40°C. After the addition of the oxanilide is completed
         (24-3 hrs), the agitation is continued 10-15 minutes. ‘The temperature is then raised tc 80°%
         over a period of on hour and maintained at 80°-85°C for 3 hours. ‘The ecid elurry is then

         cooled to room temperature and drowned by pouring over cracked ice. The product is filtered

         on a Buchner funnel and washed with water until it is almost acid free. The filter cake is
         placed in a beaker and sufficient water added to form a “slurry.” Live steam is run into the
         “slurry” under agitation for 10 minutes. The slurry is filtered and the residue washed. ‘The
         latter treatment of the "slurry" 1s repeated until the wesh water is found to be neutral to

    Yield = 90% to 97.5% of theoretical.

Origin:

     A. G. Perkin in 1892 obtained tetranitro-oxanilide directly by heating a solution of finely
powilered oxanilide in nitric acid. He also obtained the same compound by the action of a
cooled mixture of nitric and sulfuric acids on oxanilide and precipitating the product by
pouring the solution into water (J Chem Soc 61, 460 (1892).

Preparation:

     (Manufacture of Tetryl by Dinitromonomethylaniline Process, Wannamaker Chemical Cc., Inc.)

     Cg (NO,) C2 + CHIrnH, + NaQH —> Cg (NOL\), oNNyi ecH, + Nacl + 4,0

     Cgt( RO.) p7NH-CH,3 + 2HNO3 N\,      H,C-N-NO,

                                                                      + 2H,0

                                          NO,

     fo a solution of 202.5 gm dinitrochlorbenzene in 200 cc benzene, at 75°C with good sgita-
tion, in 15 to 20 minutes, add 112 gm of 30% aqueous monomethylamine. Then add 129 gm of 31%

aqueous sodium hy4roxide, in 15 to 20 minutes, at such a rate as to cause refluxing; continue

agitation for 3 hours at 70°C. ‘The mixture is concentrated to a liquid temperature of 101°-
102°¢, cooled, filtered and the precipitate washed with distilled waon} until the washings
give no test with silver nitrate, dried at 60°C (melting point 167.£°

      The dinitromethylaniline is nitrated to tetryl by solution of it in 68% sulfuric acid (197

gm nitroaniline/1190 gm sulfuric) at 25°, followed by additiou of nitric acid. ‘The process
is carried out so that the weter content remains at 16%. Solution (per 197 gm nitroaniline)
requires 5 to 10 minutes, nitration, by addition of the sulfuric acid solution to nitric acid,
about .1 hour at 30°C, plus 46 minutes at 50° to 55°C at the end. The mixture is then cooled
to 20% and filtered. ‘the tetryl is dumped into 1 liter water, washed 2 or 3 times with 200
ce coid water, and then stirred 10 to 15 minutes at 50°C with 500 ce water, filtered warm ard

then washed with water until the washings are neutral to meth:-1 orange. The tetryl dried to

constant weight at 70°C weighs about 270 gn.

     Tetryl filtered from an acid containing 87% sulfuric acid (or more) -13% water, at 40%
(or over) may fire in. 30 minutes to 1 hour and 30 minutes, if not drowmed in water. A safe

nitration procedure, even on plant scale involves:

      1. The concentration of sulfuric in the spent acid is maintained at e Low level (approx

80/1.6/18.2 sulfuric/nitric/water).

2. Nitration maximum temperature is 50°C.

3. The slurry is cooled to 35°C before filtration.

%. Filtration time prior to drowning, is minimized (15 minutes maximum).

      The crude tetryl produced is recrystallized to remove impurit’  = and oceluJed acid and to
control its granulation.

   Destruction by Chemical Decomposition:

   Tetryl is decomposed by dissolving in 12 times its weight of a solution prepared from 1

   part by weight of sodium sulfite ( RagS03°        ) in & parts water. The sulfite solution my

   be heated to 80°C to facilitate decomposition of the Tetryl.

ee ae cE   Compatibility with Metals:

                       : Copper, breéss, aluminum, magnesium, stainless steel, mild steel, mild steel coated
           with acid proof black paint and mild steel plated with copper, cadmium, zinc or nickel are
           unaffected. Magnesiun-aluminum alloy is slightly affected.

a

                 Wet: Stainlese steel and mild steel coated with scid-proof black vaint are unaffected.
           Copver, Dress, aluminum, magnesium, magnesium-aluminum alloy, mild steel and mild stee) plated
           with cadmium, copper, zinc or nickel are slightly affected.

           Preperation:

                  Tetrytols a~e manufactured by heating INT in » melting kettle, equipped with a stirrer,

           until all the INT is meltec. The necessary amount oftetryl is added and heating and stirring

           are continued. ‘The temperature is allowed to drop from 100°C uriil the mixture is of maxim
           viscosity suitable for pouring. Purt of the tetryl dissolves 1u TNT forming a eutectic mix-
           ture which contains 55 percent tetryl. Thies mixture freezes at 67.5°C.

           Origin:

                Tetrytols were developed during World War II.  The 70/30 tetryl/INT castable mixture is

           the most importent in military applications.

             It was the British work, on the kinetics of nitretion of toluene to TNT, that first pointed    meee

        out the basic importance to nitration processes of the nitroxyl ion (NOst), on the one hand,        a e
        and the role of the dDisulfate ion (890;-) and unfonized sulfuric acid on the other. These

        concepts were successful i. explaining the maximum in nitration rate occurring at a sulfuric
        acid content of 92%. ‘This vork, for instance, leada to the follcving equation for the rate of

        formation of TNT from DNT:

        2(BHT) «x (wot) [xr (H90,-) + K* (B9S0,)] (oT)

        Taree         Process: ‘Tclueue (100 gm) is nizrated to the mono derivative by slowly add1ig
        a sites CP OF oe suiturt = acid (sp gr 1-84) and 147 gm nitric acid (sp gr 1.42) to it at
        30°hO°C, with good agitation. Acid addition reqvires 1-1.5 hour, and stirring at 30°-lo°c

        is continued 30 minutes longer. The mixture is cooled and the lower leyer of spent acid

        drewn off.

            Half the crude mono is dissolved in 109 gm sulfuric acia (sp gr 1.84) with cooling, the
        soJution heated to 50°C and a mixture of 54.5 gm nitric acid (sp gr 1.50) and Sh.5 am sul~
        furic acid (sp gr 1.84) added, under agitation, at such a rate that the temperature is main-
        tained betveen 90° and 100°C. Acid addition requires 1 hour, and stirring at 909-100 is

        conti ued 2 more hours.

        . While the dinitration mixture ig still at 90°C, 145 gm fuming sulfuric acid (vleum con-
        taining 15% free 90.) is added slowly. A mixed acid of 92.5 gm each nitric acid (sp gr 1.50)
        and 15% oleum is sliviy a , under good egitation at 100%11 * over 14-2 hours. ‘The mix-

        ture is stirred at 100°-115°C for 2 mor» hours, cooled, filterea, and the INT cake broken up

        and washed with water. ‘The THT is weshed 3-4 times with kot water (85°-95°C) witk good agt-

        tation. The proé:ct can be purified either by recrystallization from alcohol or by weshing

        it with 5 times its weight of 5% sodium bisulfite solution at 90°C for 4 heur with vigorous

        stirring, washing with hot water until the weshings are colorless, and cooling slowly witb

        stirring to granulate the product.

                 iT was firat prepared in 1863 by Wilbrand (Ann 128, 178), later by Eeilstein and Kublberg

        : (Ber 3, 202 (1870, end elso Tiemann (Ber 3, 217 , 1870), enc: using different methods of stert-
            ing materials. It wes necrly 30 years later when Hausermann undertook its manufacture on an
            industrial scale (Z angew Chem, 1891, p. 508; J Chem in*, 1891, p- 1028). “After 1901 THT
           began to be used extensively as a military expiosiv< and Germany became the first nation to
            adopt it as a standard sheil filler (1902-1904). uring Vorld Wear 1 all the major powers of

             the world were using INT, with the quentity used Limited only by the available supply of
             toluene. Prior to World Wer II the development of eynthe sic toluene from petroleum made
             availadle in the United States, an almost unlimited surly of this rew material. Because of

             the general suitability of THT for melt-loading and its extensive use in >inary and ternary

             explosive mixtures, INT is considered the most important military explosive known today.

A        Preparation:

k n           Torpex is manufactured by heating TNT to approrimetely 100°C in a steam-jacketed kettle

A E      equipped with a stirrer. Water wet RDX is added sloviy to the molten INT, while mixing and
         heating, until all the water is evaporated. Aluminum is added and the mixture ia stirred
eee      until uniform. The mixture if cooled, with continued stirring, until it is suiteble for
         Fouring. Torpex can also be mad: hy adding the calculated amount of INT to Composition B
eee ne
         to maintein the desired propertion of RDX/7NT, heating and stirring, and adding 18 percent
oN penn
         cf aluminum *o complete the nixture.

ent                                                                                                             ey

               Torpex, & castable high explosive, wes developed in Exglasd during World War II for  use         o e
         asa filler in warheads, mines and depth bombs. Several variations in the composition       of

         torpex hvve been evaluated but che following are those used in © -rvice munitions:                     a

                                     torpex 2                    Torpex 2                                       eo he ®rr

         Caleium chloride, %

         (a) Made fron Composition B-2 or 60/40 Cyclctol.

         (b) Made by the addition of aluminum to Composition 8.

         (c) Made by the addition of calcium chloride to Torpex 2.

         Wax hag the undesirable eftect of (1) tending tc coagulate the aluminum, thus giving « less
         hesogeneous and more viscous product, (2) lowering the density of the cast explosive from
         1.72-1.75 to 1.56-1.70 for waxed torpex, and (3) lowering the compressive strength from 3700
         psi to 1970 psi for waxed torper. However, wax is used in service torpex for reasons of

         safety, since there is evidence that its rresence Jowers the sensitivity of the exploeive to

         impact es measured by laboratory drop tes.e and bullet sensitivity tests of small charges

         (Bureau of Ord Res Mewo Rpt No. 2h, Januaiy 1945).

                                       Trimonite, a cesteble mixture of picric acid/mononitronaphthalene was developed by the

                            British during Wor). War IT as an improvement over tridite which is a mixture of 80/20 picric

            i               acid/dinitrophenol. oth mixtures are suitable for melt-loading below 100°C and therefore

            | represent an improvement over melt-loeding picric acid alone (melting point 122°C). However,
                                        tridite is slightly inferior to picric acid as an explosive and dinitrophenol is objection-
                                         able dDecause of its toxicity. Trimonite is aiso slightly inferior to picric acid and INT as

                            an explosive. Because of the low eutectic temperature of the picric acid-mononi tronap?ithalene

                            mixture (49°C), Tridite exudes when stored at elevated temperatures. It does not possess the                   re

                            disadvantages of picric acid (corrosive action on metals, ease of decomposition, etc.} and is

                            a comparatively inexoensive substitute for TNT.

were slowly added, with etirriag, to 160 gm (2.55 ml) of 99% nitric acid at a temperature of
-25° to 0°. on equivalent weight basis, this quantity of 99% nitric acid corresponds to an
excess of 6.3 times the TPE used) After addition of the TPE, t.. reaction mixture was stirred
for about one hour at 0° to 5% and poured into eight times ite volume of cracked ice. ‘the

product, when allowed to stand overnight, was crushed under water; filtered with suction; and

washed copiously with water. It was then treated twice with about 5 times its weight of a 1%

ammonium carbonate svlution, stirred for several hours, filtered and washed with water until

the final washings were neutral to litmus. ‘The final product was washed successively with
50 cz “ach of ethanol and ether. ‘The miterial drigd in air weighed 37.8 gm or 964 of theory

based on TPE. It had a nelting range of 71° to TiC. Crystallization cf the crude TPEON frou

chloroform was found to be the most suitable method of obtaining pure TPEON.

E O               The Addition cf aluminum to increase the power of explosives wes proposed by EBaceles in

e e         1899 and patented by Roth in 1900 (German Patent 172,327). Some recent ctudies, directed
            towards establishment of the optimum amount of aluminum in the T¥T/Aluminun system, have shown
R e         that (1) the blest effect increases to a weximum vhen the elusinum content is 30% (Ref g);
            the brisance, as measured by the Sand Test, passes through a maximum at about 17% aluminua
r e         (Ref h); in Fragmentation Tests, no maximum je observed, additions of aluminum causing a de-
            crease in efficiency over the entire renge from 0% to 70% aluminum (Ref i); and (4) the rate
8 ee        of detonation of cast charges is continuously decrease? >y adfitiors of aluminum up to 4og
            (Ref 3). For ali practicel purposes .t is concluded that the addition of 18% to 20% sluninun

            to THT isproves ite performance to a mximum. This conclusion is in agreement with that of

            British workera vho measured performance of aluminized TNT-mixtures based on extensive Lead
            Block Test date (Ref x).

                 Tritonal, consisting of 80% TNT and 20% aluminum, was developed and standardized in the
            United States during world War If for use in bombs.

       Preparation:                                                                                        mone net  eae

             The preparation of this class of explosive compositions is illustrated by tle mevaod used               a e

       for Veltex No. 448: Place 675 cc of water in a slurry kettle equipped with an agit-t-~. Add                   ee
       5.85 em of 2-nitrodiphenylamine and agitate for several minutes to obtain dispersion. Then
       add 93.7 gm of water-wet nitrocellulose (dry weight 67.5 gm) in small portions. Prise the                          ge! beta:
       temperature to 48°C and maintain this temperature, but continue the agitation. A mixture uo?
       48.2 gm of nitroglycerin and 13.5 gm of triacetin is added over a 5-minutc period, with the                        EOS
       mixing continuing for an additional 10 minutes at 48°C. ‘The IMX (350 gm) ic udded over a
       5-minute period vith agitation continued for 30 minutes at 48°C ‘The slurry is cocled to

       room temperature and filtered. The filter cake is dried to a moicture cont«nt between 8% and
       12%. The incorporation of this mix is completed * rolling 50 gm portions at a terperature

       of approximately 90°C. ‘The finished coll “4 is then preheated on a heat table at GO°S. In-
       crements of 25 gm each are pressed a. 570. pei for four minutes at 71°C. A eylinier is then

       built up by pressing together four 25 eg: increments for a dwell time of 15 minutes.

                ins

             Veltex is the neme given to a series of closely releted nitrocellulose comporitions pre-
       pared in 1957 at Picatinny Arsenal by the solventless procese used for propellants. These
       compositions el] contain a high percentage of solid high explosive. They were investiga ed‘
       to determinate the suitability of the Holtex type explosive developed by Hispano Suiza of
       Switzerland, France and Spain, but for which the composition was not reported (Ref «). Com-
       positions similar to Veltex No. 448 and containing 60% to 80% HMK, with either nitroglycerin
       or triethyleneglycol dinitrate as colloiding egent for n‘*trocellulose, have also veen prepared.
       In general these compositions showed lower heat stability than that of cunventional high ex-
       plosive compositions.
